rationale: Zero-shot Jev on the same 1,000-instance samples reached AUROC 0.846 for AI-generated-text detection on RAID (noul) and macro-F1 0.531 on ESCI relevance (choice), below the zero-shot macro-F1 of the generative models named in the text (Opus 5 0.609, GLM 5.3 0.593, GPT 5.6 Terra 0.573) and above most agent-built artifacts; no interval is reported for Jev and the RAID zero-shot comparators appear only in Fig. 2 (Sec. 1, 4.1-4.2, App. E).

Jev's projected full-workload cost was $104.89 on ESCI (2.62M items) and $223.16 on RAID (5.62M) against $17,273 for zero-shot Opus 5 on ESCI, but with lower quality (0.531 vs 0.609), and agent-built artifacts reached 94% of Jev's ESCI score at 25% of its cost ($26.28) and 97% of its RAID AUROC at about 2% ($4.69); Jev cannot do generative extraction (MAVE) (Sec. 1, 4.2, Fig. 3, App. E).

Order consistency was higher for Jev than for Qwen3-32B (same answer in both presentation orders on 94.8% vs 90.6% of 500 TREC pairs and 86.7% vs 72.0% of 80,000 MS MARCO pairs), but Jev's Othello corner preference moved from 14.4% to 24.3% when the board was rendered as a coordinate list (App. G, K, N).

On 12,280 held-out chess move pairs with a non-tied Stockfish preference, Jev had the lowest ECE against Stockfish (0.081 vs DiffusionGemma 0.159, OLMo-2-32B 0.176, Qwen3-32B 0.260), although agreement was near chance for all judges (Jev 54.5%, others 52.9-54.4%) (Sec. 5.5).

Escalating Jev's 25% least-certain reranking pairs to Qwen3-32B never helped: the gated labels lost 0.047 NDCG@10 [0.013, 0.084] to Jev alone at 80,000 answers and differed by -0.007 [-0.027, 0.012] at 160,000; Qwen's labels on uncertain pairs recovered 0.004 of the 0.050 lost by dropping 20% of pairs (Sec. 6; App. N); offline label allocation, not a deployed gate.

Jev labels cost $1.97 and about 16 min of API time for 126,270 chess responses (7.6 ms/response, 20 concurrent) vs 1.91 H200 GPU-h for Qwen3-32B, and a reranker trained on Jev labels matched Qwen's (NDCG@10 0.637 vs 0.630, +0.008 [-0.007, 0.022]) from 21 min vs 5.1 GPU-h; but in chess a Jev-only evaluator added +2.8 Elo [-5.5, 11.0] over the stronger baseline vs +16.7 [9.0, 24.4] for Qwen, and Jev-trained scores weakened Othello and Connect-4 (Sec. 5.1, 6, 8, Table 4, App. G).

The authors' Qwen3.5-4B Yes-probability verifier (BCE-trained on 2,477 examples) reached 95.24% balanced accuracy on 936 held-out reference-bound atomic judgments (untuned 84.14%), but its candidate rankings agreed with blinded human preferences on 63.49% of 126 pairs vs 60.32% for direct Qwen3.5-27B scoring (difference CI [-8.33, 16.67]) and did not lower severe identity risk in the top candidate (47.62% vs 45.24%) (Tables 2-3, Sec. 5.2-5.3).

Keeping per-question Yes probabilities exposed which identity and relation conditions a candidate failed in one post-hoc case where the holistic 27B score chose the human's last-ranked image (Fig. 3), but the arithmetic mean lets strong scores compensate for a failed critical condition and identity risk was not reduced (47.62%); no systematic test of the audit trail (Sec. 3.5, 5.3, 7).

On 600 held-out command questions, shuffling option order cut accuracy for Strands Decider 2B (0.59 to 0.38), Kev 9B (0.60 to 0.50) and Laya base (0.56 to 0.49) but not Clef-Flash 9B (0.54 to 0.54), and Kev 4B weapon accuracy fell 0.97 to 0.62; all zero-shot typed models but Kev 0.8B chose 'collect' 1.6-1.8 times chance among errors in either order, as did Qwen3.6 without reasoning (1.8) but less with reasoning (1.4) (Table 1, Sec. 5.1).

Zero-shot typed models had command ECE 0.10-0.57 and confidence AUROC 0.45-0.89 (fixed order) with no link between calibration and sensitivity; typed-decisions Laya, Strands and Kev 9B were under-confident (mean top probability 0.31-0.42 at accuracy 0.59-0.60), and the most sensitive model (Laya base, AUROC 0.89 [0.85, 0.92]) was at chance within categories (0.52 [0.40, 0.63]) and fell to 0.72 with shuffled options (Table 2, Sec. 5.2).

Deferring the 30% least-confident decisions to reasoning Qwen3.6 beat random deferral by +0.13 [0.08, 0.18] with actor and rate chosen on held-out games (+0.08 [0.02, 0.14] with shuffled options) and matched the thinker alone at 30% of its calls (0.75 vs 0.69, +0.06 [-0.02, 0.11]), but gave nothing for Kev 9B and Strands (AUROC 0.61, 0.60) and never beat the better component (+0.05 [-0.12, 0.11]); in 33 closed-loop games a fixed explore rule behind the same gate covered as much ground (Tables 3-4, Sec. 5.3-5.4).

On 43,496 Chinese-language typed questions, the authors' Chip (Kev-0.8B fine-tuned on 88,604 records) had ECE 0.0032 and hosted JEV 0.0271 vs 0.0307-0.0607 for three flagship LLMs' stated probabilities (Gemma3 0.0225 on its valid records), but Chip's calibration did not transfer to JevBench (ECE 0.1633 Original, 0.3577 Hard vs JEV 0.0947) (Tables 3-4).

Mean latency was 118 ms for Chip and 1,510 ms for JEV vs 4,631-16,009 ms for flagship LLMs, but JEV failed 678 of 5,000 records and reached 84.52% FFD exact match vs 98.32-99.12% for the flagships, and Chip's 99.32% needed task training on 88,604 records (Tables 3, 6, 9; Sec. 3.2.1).

With physical features Jev's yes/no fault question flagged 75-99% of fault windows but also 57-94% of fault-free ones (AUROC 0.65; condition answer 0.68), under the nine shift tests no model beat flagging every window (detection F1 0.71; Jev 0.67-0.70), and pooled diagnosis of consistency faults was 37% vs 46% for Qwen2.5 72B, which erred like Jev on detection (Table 5, Sec. 4.1-4.2, 4.4).

Rewording the three questions changed 3-6% of Jev's answers and irrelevant fields 2-6%, but class names without definitions changed 41% (ORNL consistency accuracy 71% to 6%), a same-content paraphrase of the definitions changed 8-9% and moved context-fault accuracy 13% to 43%, and shuffling state-field order changed 13% of RP-1312 answers and made the yes/no question flag 94% of fault-free windows (Sec. 4.1).

Pooled shifted ECE was 0.27 [0.21, 0.36] for Jev vs 0.43 for Qwen2.5 72B, 0.60 for 7B and 0.36 for LightGBM, and did not drift under shift (+0.01 [-0.09, 0.09]), but windows at stated 0.94 were right 62% of the time, temperature scaling (0.28 to 0.17) overshot into underconfidence, the yes/no and condition answers contradicted each other (84% 'fault' vs 95% 'normal' on ORNL fault-free windows), and Jev gave its top answer >=0.7 on 63% of fault windows with no physical trace (Sec. 4.2, 4.4, 4.6, Fig. 4).

190,582 Jev requests cost US$18.69 (0.19 s mean, 0.26 s p95; about US$3.40 per unit-year at 15-min checks) vs about 2 s per window for local Qwen2.5 72B at no per-query cost but with data kept on site, and the study confines the model to ranking candidate faults from code-computed features with recalibration and an operator's final call (Sec. 4.7, 5.4).

Human coders confirmed 96-100% of Jev flags (p>=0.5) where the coded field also recorded the factor but only 15% (13 flags) for unbelted occupants, 26% (27) for wrong-way driving, 52-57% for drugs and medical episodes and 71-90% for alcohol, fatigue, hydroplaning and phone use where it did not (Table B.2; Sec. 6); counts are small and intervals wide.

Jev's raw probabilities overstated the human rate so that the identity map failed the held-out unbiasedness rule for 14 of 15 factors (all but vehicle defects); Platt or isotonic maps fitted on 2,309 judgments cut held-out Brier (x1000), e.g. alcohol 4.56 to 2.71 and hit-and-run 7.44 to 5.84, and the recalibrated counts then agreed with an independent blinded human tier for all 15 factors (App. B, Table B.2; Sec. 5.1).

Jev read 229,510 sampled narratives of a 5,018,080-crash population (reading all would cost about $773), and a second blinded human tier agreed with all 15 statewide counts within its margin (phone use 15,074 vs check 16,211 [13,050, 19,371]), but only after per-factor human recalibration that carries most of the variance (95% for alcohol, 99% for wrong-way) (Tables 2, 4; Sec. 5.1-5.2).
